1.uses: Thuja 'Smaragd' is the landscapers' first choice for elegant hedges in residential developments, private gardens, commercial sites and company headquarters. Its narrow columnar shape takes up little space – ideal for small plots and along fences – and its emerald-green colour lasts through winter without turning bronze like other thuja varieties. It is also used in double rows for privacy screens, as a vertical accent at entrances or in large containers on terraces.
1.planting: For a dense hedge, 2–3 plants per linear metre are usually planted (35–50 cm apart), depending on the height of the plants delivered. The planting hole should be twice as wide as the root ball; after planting, water thoroughly and mulch with bark. Container plants can be planted from spring to autumn, avoiding frost and heatwaves.
1.care: Thuja 'Smaragd' grows moderately (about 20–30 cm per year) and does not need frequent trimming – one light correction a year is enough. In the first two years after planting it needs regular watering, especially in summer; prolonged drought is the main cause of browning. A spring feed with conifer fertiliser keeps the colour intense.

faq.q: How tall does Thuja 'Smaragd' grow?
faq.a: At maturity it usually reaches 4–5 m in height and 1–1.5 m in width, but it can be kept at the desired hedge height by trimming.

faq.q: Which sizes of Thuja 'Smaragd' do you supply wholesale?
faq.a: We have Thuja 'Smaragd' in several heights. Send us the height and quantity you need and we will confirm availability and price.

2.uses: Yew (Taxus baccata) is the preferred conifer for geometrically clipped hedges, topiary (spheres, cubes, cones) and evergreen borders in formal gardens, historic parks and premium landscaping. It is one of the few conifers that tolerates shade well, so it is used on the north side of buildings, under large trees and in courtyards. Note: all parts of the plant (except the red flesh around the seeds) are toxic, so it is not recommended next to playgrounds or pastures.
2.planting: For hedges, 3–4 plants per linear metre are planted, depending on size. Yew prefers well-drained soils and does not tolerate waterlogging. Container plants can be planted almost all year round; water well after planting and mulch.
2.care: Growth is slow (about 15–20 cm per year), but yew has a rare advantage among conifers: it regenerates from old wood, so it can be cut back hard and reshaped. Trimming is done once or twice a year, usually in early summer. It is very long-lived and needs minimal maintenance once established.

faq.q: Is yew suitable for public spaces?
faq.a: Yes, in parks and formal gardens, but avoid planting it next to children's playgrounds or areas with animals, as the leaves and seeds are toxic.

faq.q: Does yew grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, yew is one of the most shade-tolerant conifers and grows well in both partial and full shade.

3.uses: Black pine (Pinus nigra) is a robust tree for parks, shelterbelts, roadside plantings, slopes and low-maintenance green spaces. It tolerates drought, wind, calcareous soils and urban pollution better than most conifers, which is why it is widely used in public projects and in regions with a harsh continental climate. As a solitary specimen it has an imposing silhouette with a dense, dark-green crown.
3.planting: As a solitary tree it needs space – at maturity it exceeds 15–20 m. For shelterbelts it is planted in rows, 3–4 m apart. It prefers sunny sites and adapts to soils from sandy to clay, as long as they are not permanently waterlogged.
3.care: Once established, black pine needs very little care: watering only in the first years and during very dry periods after planting. It requires no pruning apart from removing dead branches or those obstructing paths and roads.

faq.q: Is black pine drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant pines, suitable for sunny sites and poor soils.

faq.q: Is black pine suitable for shelterbelts?
faq.a: Yes, its dense crown and wind resistance make it very good for shelterbelts and windbreaks.

4.uses: Oriental thuja (Platycladus orientalis) is an excellent alternative to common thuja in hot, dry regions and very sunny urban spaces. Its vertical, fan-shaped branches give it a distinctive decorative texture. It is used for hedges, screens, rows along paths and in cemeteries, where it is valued for its neat appearance all year round.
4.planting: For hedges, 2–3 plants per linear metre are planted. It prefers sunny sites and well-drained soils, including calcareous ones. Water well after planting and repeat during dry spells in the first year.
4.care: It tolerates drought better than Thuja occidentalis, but needs regular watering in the first years for good rooting. It can be lightly trimmed in spring or summer to keep its shape; hard cuts into old wood should be avoided.

faq.q: What is the difference between oriental thuja and Thuja 'Smaragd'?
faq.a: Oriental thuja has vertical fan-shaped branches and tolerates drought and heat better, while Thuja 'Smaragd' has a narrower columnar shape and prefers moister soils.

faq.q: Is oriental thuja suitable for dry areas?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the best conifers for hedges in hot, dry areas.

5.uses: Blue spruce (Picea pungens 'Glauca') is a showpiece tree for squares, parks, building entrances, corporate headquarters and large gardens. The silvery-blue colour of its needles contrasts strongly with other plants, so it is used as a focal point. Many cities also plant it as a living Christmas tree in public spaces, decorated year after year.
5.planting: Blue spruce needs space: at maturity it reaches 10–15 m in height and 4–6 m in width, so it should be planted at least 4–5 m from buildings and other trees. It prefers sunny sites and slightly acidic, well-drained soils.
5.care: It is very frost-hardy and needs no pruning; only dead branches at the base may be removed. In the first years after planting, water regularly during dry spells. In very hot, dry summers it can be attacked by spider mites, so watering and periodic checks are recommended.

faq.q: How big does blue spruce grow?
faq.a: In cultivation it usually reaches 10–15 m in height, with a broad conical crown 4–6 m wide.

faq.q: Can blue spruce be used as a Christmas tree in public spaces?
faq.a: Yes, thanks to its regular conical shape and striking colour it is very well suited as a living Christmas tree in squares and parks.

6.uses: Creeping juniper (Juniperus horizontalis) is one of the best solutions for covering large areas with minimal maintenance: slopes, roundabouts, public squares, car parks, rock gardens and path edges. It forms a dense carpet 15–30 cm high that stabilises soil on slopes, prevents erosion and suppresses weeds. It is widely used in public green-space projects precisely because of its low maintenance costs.
6.planting: Each plant eventually spreads 1.5–2.5 m. Depending on plant size and how quickly you want coverage, 1–3 plants per square metre are usually planted. Until the carpet closes, mulch the area with bark or use weed-control fabric.
6.care: Once established it tolerates drought, heat and poor soils very well. It needs no pruning apart from shoots growing over kerbs or paths. Wet soils where water stagnates should be avoided, as the roots can rot there.

faq.q: How many creeping juniper plants are needed per square metre?
faq.a: Usually 1–3 plants per m², depending on the size of the plants and how quickly you want full coverage.

faq.q: Is creeping juniper suitable for slopes?
faq.a: Yes, its roots and dense carpet hold the soil on slopes and reduce erosion, which is why it is widely used on slopes and roundabouts.

7.uses: Catalpa (Catalpa bignonioides) is a classic shade tree for boulevards, street plantings, parks, school yards and squares. Its broad crown and large heart-shaped leaves give dense shade in summer, and in June–July the tree is covered with fragrant white flowers. It tolerates urban conditions well – pollution, compacted soils and heat – which is why it is common in cities.
7.planting: Catalpa reaches 10–15 m in height with an equally wide crown. In avenues it is planted 8–10 m apart. It prefers sunny sites and fertile soils but adapts to most soil types. For narrow streets, globe-shaped forms are often used – ask us about availability.
7.care: After planting, trees are staked and watered regularly for the first two years. Catalpa comes into leaf late, only in May, which is normal for this species. Formative pruning is done at the end of winter, and dead branches are removed periodically.

faq.q: Is catalpa suitable for street plantings?
faq.a: Yes, catalpa is widely used for avenues and boulevards thanks to its broad crown and tolerance of urban conditions.

faq.q: When does catalpa flower?
faq.a: Catalpa flowers in June–July with large clusters of fragrant white flowers, followed by long decorative pods.

8.uses: Magnolia grandiflora is a spectacular evergreen tree with large glossy leaves and huge, intensely fragrant white flowers in summer. It is a prestigious choice for hotel entrances, villas, corporate headquarters, Mediterranean gardens and luxury landscaping. It remains decorative in winter, when most trees are bare.
8.planting: Hardy to about -12°C, Magnolia grandiflora does best in regions with mild winters, in sites sheltered from cold winds, for example next to south-facing buildings. It prefers slightly acidic to neutral, rich, well-drained soils. Planting is done in spring so the plant can root before its first winter.
8.care: In the first years it needs regular watering and mulching to keep the soil moist. Young specimens are protected with horticultural fleece in severe winters. Pruning is limited to removing damaged branches.

faq.q: Can Magnolia grandiflora survive Romanian winters?
faq.a: It is hardy to about -12°C. It suits regions with mild winters and sheltered sites; in colder areas winter protection is recommended.

faq.q: Does Magnolia grandiflora keep its leaves in winter?
faq.a: Yes, it is an evergreen magnolia and keeps its glossy leaves all year.

9.uses: Cherry laurel (Prunus laurocerasus) is one of the most widely used hedge shrubs in Europe. Its large, glossy, evergreen leaves quickly form a dense visual and noise screen, ideal for property boundaries, residential developments, car parks and commercial sites. It tolerates shade, pollution and urban conditions, so it also suits courtyards and spaces between apartment blocks.
9.planting: For hedges, 2–3 plants per linear metre are usually planted, depending on plant size. It adapts to most soils but does not tolerate waterlogging. Water thoroughly after planting and mulch.
9.care: Cherry laurel grows fast (about 30–50 cm per year), so the hedge is trimmed once or twice a year, usually after flowering and at the end of summer. It regenerates well after pruning. The fruit and leaves are toxic if ingested, which should be considered near playgrounds.

faq.q: How fast does cherry laurel grow?
faq.a: Cherry laurel grows about 30–50 cm per year, making it one of the fastest evergreen hedge plants.

faq.q: Does cherry laurel grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates partial and even full shade well, so it suits courtyards and shaded areas.

10.uses: Photinia 'Red Robin' (Photinia × fraseri) is valued for its bright red young shoots, which appear in spring and after every trim. It is used for colourful hedges, screens, tall borders, as a solitary shrub or trained as a standard, in residential developments, at company headquarters and in commercial spaces. Combined with cherry laurel or thuja, it creates hedges with colour accents.
10.planting: For hedges, 2–3 plants per linear metre are planted. It prefers sunny or partly shaded sites and well-drained soils. In regions with harsh winters, plant it in sites sheltered from cold winds.
10.care: Trimming two or three times a year stimulates new red shoots. The plant is hardy to about -15°C; in very cold winters the tips may be damaged but recover in spring. In wet summers leaf spot may appear, so well-drained soil and enough spacing for air circulation are recommended.

faq.q: How do you keep the red colour of Photinia 'Red Robin'?
faq.a: By regular trimming: after each trim the plant produces new red shoots, so 2–3 trims a year keep the colour intense.

faq.q: How many Photinia plants are needed per metre of hedge?
faq.a: Usually 2–3 plants per linear metre, depending on plant size.

11.uses: Fountain grass (Pennisetum alopecuroides) is an ornamental grass widely used in modern and naturalistic landscaping: roundabouts, park beds, borders, office courtyards and low-maintenance gardens. It forms compact clumps of arching leaves, and from late summer to autumn produces soft, fluffy plumes that move beautifully in the wind. It stays decorative in winter, when the dry clumps catch the frost.
11.planting: Depending on variety and size, 3–5 plants per square metre are planted. It prefers sunny sites and well-drained soils. Plant in spring or early autumn; in large groups it creates a very decorative mass effect.
11.care: Once established it tolerates drought well. Clumps are cut back close to the ground at the end of winter or in early spring, not in autumn, to keep their winter interest. Every few years large clumps can be divided.

faq.q: When should fountain grass be cut back?
faq.a: At the end of winter or in early spring, before new growth starts, to 10–15 cm above the ground.

faq.q: Is Pennisetum suitable for public spaces?
faq.a: Yes, it is hardy, drought tolerant and needs only one cut a year, which is why it is widely used on roundabouts and in parks.

12.uses: Bamboo quickly creates dense privacy screens with an exotic, modern look for restaurant terraces, hotels, courtyards, Zen gardens and modern residential projects. It is very well suited to large planters on terraces and roofs, where it replaces conventional fences. Its foliage moves in the wind and creates a calm atmosphere.
12.planting: For screens, 1–2 plants per linear metre are usually planted, depending on size. There are two types of bamboo: running types (for example Phyllostachys), which spread and must be planted with a rhizome barrier, and clumping types (for example Fargesia), which do not spread. We will recommend the right type for your project.
12.care: Bamboo prefers rich, moist soils and needs regular watering, especially in planters and in the first years. Frost hardiness depends on the species, down to about -15°C. Old or dead canes are removed in spring.

faq.q: Does bamboo spread in the garden?
faq.a: Running species spread and need a rhizome barrier; clumping species such as Fargesia do not spread.

faq.q: Can bamboo be grown in planters on terraces?
faq.a: Yes, bamboo is very well suited to large planters, provided it is watered regularly.

13.uses: Hydrangea is one of the most spectacular flowering shrubs for gardens, building entrances, restaurant and hotel terraces, shady beds and planters. Its large round or conical flower heads in white, pink, blue or red decorate from June until autumn. It is used in groups, as a border or as a solitary shrub in the shaded parts of a scheme.
13.planting: Plant 80–100 cm apart, in partly shaded sites protected from strong afternoon sun. It prefers humus-rich, moist, well-drained soils. In some varieties flower colour depends on soil pH – in acidic soils the flowers can turn blue.
13.care: Hydrangea needs frequent watering, especially in summer – wilting leaves are the first sign of water shortage. Mulching helps retain moisture. Pruning depends on the variety: some flower on the previous year's wood and are only lightly trimmed, others flower on new wood and can be cut back harder in spring.

faq.q: Should hydrangea be planted in sun or shade?
faq.a: It does best in partial shade, protected from strong afternoon sun, in moist, rich soil.

faq.q: Why does hydrangea change its flower colour?
faq.a: In some varieties the colour depends on soil acidity: in acidic soils flowers tend towards blue, in neutral or alkaline soils towards pink.

14.uses: Common ivy (Hedera helix) is an evergreen climber for covering walls, fences, pergolas and posts, and also an excellent ground cover in shaded areas under trees where lawn will not grow. It is used in parks, courtyards, green walls and planters, staying green all year.
14.planting: As ground cover, 4–6 plants per square metre are planted; for covering walls or fences, 2–3 plants per linear metre. It adapts to almost any soil and prefers partial or full shade.
14.care: Ivy climbs walls by itself using aerial roots. On walls with damaged render and on young trees it should be controlled by pruning so it does not harm them. It tolerates pruning at any time during the growing season. It needs regular watering in the first year, then becomes very tough.

faq.q: How many ivy plants are needed per square metre?
faq.a: As ground cover, 4–6 plants per m² are planted, depending on plant size and how quickly you want coverage.

faq.q: Does ivy grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, ivy is one of the best plants for deep shade, including under large trees.

15.uses: Box-leaf honeysuckle (Lonicera nitida) forms low hedges and dense borders with small, glossy, evergreen leaves. It is increasingly used as an alternative to box (Buxus), which is badly affected by the box tree moth. It suits formal gardens, path edging, parks, school yards and residential landscaping.
15.planting: For borders and low hedges, 3–4 plants per linear metre are planted. It tolerates sun and partial shade and adapts to most soils. Planting can be done from spring to autumn.
15.care: It grows fast and tolerates repeated trimming very well – two or three times a year for crisply shaped borders. It is hardy to about -15°C. In the first year after planting, water regularly during dry spells.

faq.q: Can Lonicera nitida replace box?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most popular alternatives to box for borders and low hedges, without the problems caused by the box tree moth.

faq.q: How often is Lonicera nitida trimmed?
faq.a: For precisely shaped borders it is trimmed 2–3 times a year during the growing season.

16.uses: Heuchera (coral bells) is valued above all for its foliage: leaves in shades of green, burgundy, purple, caramel or silver, decorative almost all year. It is used in shady beds, borders, planters, at the base of trees and in combinations with hosta, ferns and ornamental grasses in gardens and green spaces at offices or hotels.
16.planting: Plant 5–7 plants per square metre in partly shaded sites and rich, well-drained soils. The crown (base of the plant) should not be buried too deep.
16.care: Heuchera needs constant moisture but does not tolerate waterlogging, especially in winter. Every 3–4 years clumps can be divided in spring to rejuvenate them. Dead leaves are removed in spring. It is hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: Does heuchera grow in sun?
faq.a: Most varieties prefer partial shade; in strong sun the leaves can scorch, especially if the soil is dry.

faq.q: Is heuchera decorative in winter?
faq.a: Yes, in many varieties the leaves stay decorative through winter.

17.uses: Rose of Sharon (Hibiscus syriacus) is a hardy flowering shrub that blooms profusely in the second half of summer, from July to September, when few other plants are in flower. It is used as a solitary shrub, in groups, as a flowering hedge or trained as a standard, in parks, gardens, avenues and commercial spaces.
17.planting: For a flowering hedge, 1–2 plants per linear metre are planted; as a solitary shrub leave 1.5–2 m between plants. It prefers sunny sites and fertile, well-drained soils.
17.care: Hibiscus comes into leaf late in spring, usually only in May – this is normal and does not mean the plant has been killed by frost. Pruning is done at the end of winter, as flowers appear on new wood. Regular watering in summer ensures abundant flowering.

faq.q: When does rose of Sharon flower?
faq.a: It flowers from July to September with white, pink, purple or blue flowers, depending on the variety.

faq.q: Why does hibiscus come into leaf so late?
faq.a: It is a characteristic of the species: Hibiscus syriacus starts growing late, usually in May.

18.uses: Spiraea is a hardy, easy-care flowering shrub widely used in commercial green spaces, parks, car parks, borders and low hedges. Compact species such as Spiraea japonica form low mounds with pink flowers in summer, while taller species flower profusely in spring with white flowers. It is a safe choice for schemes with a low maintenance budget.
18.planting: Compact species are planted at 3–5 plants per square metre for mass planting, or 2–3 plants per linear metre for borders. Spiraea tolerates sun and partial shade and adapts to most soils.
18.care: Summer-flowering species are pruned in early spring; spring-flowering species are pruned right after flowering. Spiraea is very frost-hardy (to about -25°C) and, once established, also tolerates dry periods.

faq.q: When should spiraea be pruned?
faq.a: Summer-flowering species (for example Spiraea japonica) are pruned in early spring; spring-flowering species after flowering.

faq.q: Is spiraea suitable for public spaces?
faq.a: Yes, it is hardy, tolerates urban conditions and needs minimal maintenance.

19.uses: Mugo pine on stem is a decorative conifer grafted onto a straight trunk, with a compact, rounded crown. It is ideal for small gardens, front yards, entrances, terraces and green roofs, as well as large containers. It is used as an accent in Japanese gardens, rock gardens and modern minimalist landscaping.
19.planting: Plant in sunny sites in well-drained soils; it also tolerates poor or calcareous soils. In containers, use a free-draining substrate. After planting, support the stem with a stake for the first years.
19.care: To keep the crown compact, shorten the new shoots (the so-called 'candles') by a third to a half in spring. It is very frost- and drought-hardy, needing watering only in the first years and in containers.

faq.q: How do you keep the crown of a mugo pine standard compact?
faq.a: By shortening the new shoots ('candles') in spring by a third to a half of their length.

faq.q: Can a mugo pine on stem be grown in a container?
faq.a: Yes, it is very well suited to large containers on terraces and roofs, with a well-drained substrate.

20.uses: Peony (Paeonia) is one of the most loved garden flowers, with large, fragrant blooms in late spring. It is used in beds, borders, traditional gardens and parks. It is extremely long-lived – a well-established clump can flower for decades in the same spot – and its foliage stays decorative after flowering.
20.planting: The ideal planting time is autumn (September–October), but container plants can also be planted in spring. The buds at the base must not be buried deeper than 3–5 cm – planting too deep is the main reason peonies fail to flower. Leave 60–90 cm between plants.
20.care: Peony prefers sunny sites and fertile, well-drained soils. It dislikes being moved, so choose the site from the start. Stems with large flowers may need supports. In autumn, after the foliage yellows, the stems are cut back to ground level.

faq.q: Why is my peony not flowering?
faq.a: The most common cause is planting too deep; the buds should be no more than 3–5 cm below soil level. Deep shade can also be a cause.

faq.q: When are peonies planted?
faq.a: Ideally in autumn, in September–October; container plants can also be planted in spring.

21.uses: Bugle (Ajuga reptans) is a low ground-cover perennial forming a dense carpet of green, bronze or purple leaves, with spikes of blue flowers in April–June. It is ideal for shaded areas under trees, path edges, gentle slopes and places where lawn does not grow well.
21.planting: Plant 9–12 plants per square metre for quick coverage. It prefers partial or full shade and soils that stay slightly moist. It spreads by runners, filling the gaps between plants.
21.care: Ajuga needs very little maintenance. In dry periods it needs watering, especially in sunnier spots. After flowering, spent spikes can be cut off. If it spreads too much, runners are easily removed.

faq.q: How many Ajuga plants are needed per square metre?
faq.a: Usually 9–12 plants per m² for full coverage within one season.

faq.q: Can Ajuga replace lawn in shade?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the best lawn alternatives in shaded areas that are not walked on often.

22.uses: Astilbe is an elegant perennial for shady, moist areas, with feathery plumes in pink, red, white and purple in summer. It is used in shady beds, on the banks of ponds and lakes, in woodland gardens and on the north side of buildings, combined with hosta and ferns.
22.planting: Plant 5–7 plants per square metre in partial or full shade, in rich soils that stay moist. In strong sun and dry soil the leaf edges dry out.
22.care: Astilbe needs regular watering, especially in summer; mulching helps keep moisture in. The dry flower heads can be left over winter as they are decorative, and in spring the stems are cut to ground level. Every 3–4 years clumps can be divided.

faq.q: Does astilbe grow in sun?
faq.a: Astilbe prefers partial or full shade; in sun it only grows if the soil stays permanently moist.

faq.q: When does astilbe flower?
faq.a: Astilbe flowers in summer, usually from June to August, depending on the variety.

23.uses: Japanese sedge 'Ice Dance' (Carex morrowii) is an evergreen ornamental grass with green, white-edged leaves that brighten shaded areas. It is used as ground cover under trees, in borders, rock gardens and planters, staying decorative in winter.
23.planting: Plant 5–7 plants per square metre. It prefers partial or full shade and moist but well-drained soils. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes, forming a dense carpet over time.
23.care: It is a very low-maintenance plant. In spring, leaves damaged over winter are removed. In dry periods it needs watering. It is hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: Does Carex 'Ice Dance' keep its leaves in winter?
faq.a: Yes, it is an evergreen ornamental grass and stays decorative all year.

faq.q: Where should Carex 'Ice Dance' be planted?
faq.a: In partial or full shade, under trees, in borders and planters, in moist, well-drained soil.

24.uses: Blue fescue (Festuca glauca) forms compact, rounded tufts of fine, silvery-blue leaves that are decorative all year. It is widely used in rock gardens, modern gravel schemes, borders, green roofs and low-maintenance green spaces, where it contrasts nicely with green or burgundy foliage.
24.planting: Plant 7–9 plants per square metre. It needs full sun and poor, dry, well-drained soils – in heavy, wet soils the tufts rot. The blue colour is most intense in sunny sites.
24.care: In spring, dead leaves are removed by combing the tuft by hand. Every 2–3 years, tufts that die out in the middle are divided and replanted. It needs no fertiliser and, once established, tolerates drought very well.

faq.q: Why does Festuca glauca die out in the middle?
faq.a: It is a natural ageing process; tufts are rejuvenated by dividing them every 2–3 years.

faq.q: Does Festuca glauca tolerate drought?
faq.a: Yes, once established it tolerates drought very well and prefers dry, poor soils.

25.uses: Daylily (Hemerocallis) is one of the toughest perennials for green spaces: it tolerates heat, drought, poor soils and urban conditions. It is used on slopes, roundabouts, park beds, borders and along roads. Each flower lasts only one day, but a clump keeps producing new flowers for several weeks in summer.
25.planting: Plant 4–6 plants per square metre. It prefers full sun or light partial shade and adapts to almost any soil. Planting can be done from spring to autumn.
25.care: Daylily needs very little care. Spent flower stems and dead leaves are cut back in autumn or spring. Every 4–5 years very dense clumps can be divided to keep flowering abundant.

faq.q: Is daylily suitable for slopes?
faq.a: Yes, its dense roots hold the soil and the plant tolerates drought, so it is widely used on slopes and in public spaces.

faq.q: How long does daylily flower?
faq.a: Each flower lasts one day, but the clump flowers continuously for several weeks in summer; there are also repeat-flowering varieties.

26.uses: Hosta is the 'queen of shade': its large decorative leaves in green, blue, yellow or variegated shades turn shaded areas into spectacular beds. It is used under trees, on the north side of buildings, in courtyards, woodland gardens and planters, combined with astilbe, ferns and heuchera.
26.planting: Depending on the size of the variety, 3–5 plants per square metre are planted. It prefers partial or full shade and rich, moist but well-drained soils.
26.care: Hosta needs regular watering in dry periods. The main pests are slugs and snails, which can hole the leaves in spring, so monitoring is recommended. In autumn the foliage dies back and the plant reshoots every spring. It is very frost-hardy, to about -30°C.

faq.q: Does hosta grow in deep shade?
faq.a: Yes, hosta is one of the best perennials for shade; blue-leaved varieties especially prefer shade.

faq.q: Does hosta stay green in winter?
faq.a: No, hosta dies back in autumn and starts growing again in spring.

27.uses: Bearded iris (Iris germanica) is a classic, drought-tolerant perennial with large, elegant flowers in late spring in purple, blue, white, yellow and bicolours. It is used in sunny beds, borders, traditional gardens, slopes and public green spaces. Its sword-shaped leaves stay decorative after flowering.
27.planting: Plant 6–9 plants per square metre. The rhizomes are planted at the surface, half exposed – planting too deep leads to rot and no flowers. It needs full sun and well-drained soil.
27.care: Once established, iris tolerates drought very well and should not be overwatered. Every 3–4 years, after flowering (July–August), dense clumps are divided and replanted. Dead leaves are removed in autumn.

faq.q: How deep should bearded iris be planted?
faq.a: The rhizomes are planted at the surface, half exposed; planting too deep prevents flowering.

faq.q: When are irises divided?
faq.a: Every 3–4 years, after flowering, usually in July–August.

28.uses: Red hot poker (Kniphofia uvaria) is an exotic perennial with tall, torch-shaped flower spikes in orange-red to yellow in summer. It is a spectacular vertical accent in sunny beds, gravel gardens, modern schemes and Mediterranean gardens, and also attracts pollinators.
28.planting: Plant 3–5 plants per square metre in full sun and well-drained soil. Drainage is essential especially in winter, when excess moisture can kill the plant.
28.care: It tolerates drought once established. Spent flower stems are cut after flowering. In regions with cold winters, the leaves can be tied together over the crown in autumn to protect it from wet, and the base mulched. Old leaves are cleaned up in spring.

faq.q: When does Kniphofia flower?
faq.a: It flowers in summer, usually from June to September, depending on the variety.

faq.q: How is Kniphofia protected in winter?
faq.a: Provide well-drained soil, mulch the base and tie the leaves over the crown to keep it dry.

29.uses: Mondo grass (Ophiopogon japonicus) is an evergreen ground cover with narrow, dark-green leaves forming a dense, lawn-like carpet that needs no mowing. It is used between paving stones, in Japanese gardens, borders, under trees and in shaded courtyards.
29.planting: For full coverage, 9–16 plants per square metre are planted, as it spreads slowly. It prefers partial or full shade and moist, well-drained soils.
29.care: It needs no mowing or cutting; damaged leaves can be removed in spring. In dry periods it must be watered. It is hardy to about -15°C, so sheltered sites are recommended in cold regions.

faq.q: Can Ophiopogon replace lawn?
faq.a: Yes, in shaded, lightly used areas it forms an evergreen carpet without mowing.

faq.q: How many Ophiopogon plants are needed per square metre?
faq.a: Between 9 and 16 plants per m², as the plant spreads slowly.

30.uses: White obedient plant (Physostegia virginiana 'Alba') is a perennial with elegant spikes of white flowers from July to September. Its name comes from the fact that the flowers stay in whatever position they are moved to. It is used in beds, borders, naturalistic gardens and for cut flowers.
30.planting: Plant 5–7 plants per square metre in sun or partial shade, in moist, fertile soils. It spreads by rhizomes and can become vigorous, so leave room or use an edging barrier.
30.care: It needs watering in dry periods. Stems are cut to ground level in autumn or spring. Every few years clumps are divided to control spreading.

faq.q: When does Physostegia flower?
faq.a: It flowers in the second half of summer, from July to September.

faq.q: Does Physostegia spread in the garden?
faq.a: Yes, it spreads by rhizomes; periodic division or an edging barrier is recommended.

31.uses: Sedum rupestre 'Angelina' is a succulent ground cover with golden-yellow, needle-like leaves that turn orange in autumn and winter. It is one of the most used plants for extensive green roofs, rock gardens, retaining walls, planters and sunny, low-maintenance public spaces.
31.planting: Plant 9–12 plants per square metre. It needs full sun and a poor, very well-drained substrate; on green roofs a special substrate is used.
31.care: Once established it tolerates extreme drought and needs no fertiliser. Standing water is the only thing that can kill it. Broken pieces root easily, which helps fill gaps quickly.

faq.q: Is Sedum 'Angelina' suitable for green roofs?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the key species for extensive green roofs thanks to its drought and heat tolerance.

faq.q: How many Sedum plants are needed per square metre?
faq.a: Usually 9–12 plants per m² for quick coverage.

32.uses: Sedum hybridum is a succulent ground-cover perennial with deep-green leaves and yellow summer flowers. It forms a dense, tough carpet used on extensive green roofs, slopes, rock gardens and sunny public spaces where irrigation is limited.
32.planting: Plant 9–12 plants per square metre in full sun on poor, well-drained soils. It also adapts to the thin substrates used on roofs.
32.care: It is extremely frost-hardy (to about -30°C) and drought tolerant. It needs no fertiliser or pruning; after flowering, spent flower heads can be trimmed for a tidy look.

faq.q: Is Sedum hybridum frost-hardy?
faq.a: Yes, it is very frost-hardy, down to about -30°C.

faq.q: Where is Sedum hybridum used?
faq.a: On green roofs, slopes, rock gardens and sunny public spaces with limited irrigation.

33.uses: Sedum rupestre 'Blue' has blue-grey, needle-like leaves that contrast beautifully with Sedum 'Angelina' and other green succulents. It is used on green roofs, in rock gardens, planters and modern gravel schemes.
33.planting: Plant 9–12 plants per square metre in full sun and dry, well-drained soil. Combined in bands or patches with other sedum species, it creates decorative patterns over large areas.
33.care: It needs minimal maintenance: no fertiliser and no watering after establishment, except during very long droughts. Wet, heavy soils should be avoided.

faq.q: What does Sedum rupestre 'Blue' combine well with?
faq.a: It combines very well with golden Sedum 'Angelina' and other green succulents for colour contrast.

faq.q: Does Sedum 'Blue' need watering?
faq.a: Hardly at all once established; water only during very prolonged drought.

34.uses: Sedum 'Watson' is a decorative succulent forming rosettes in shades of pink and green, attractive all year. It is used in rock gardens, planters, decorative pots, green roofs and succulent combinations.
34.planting: Plant 9–12 plants per square metre in full sun on a poor, very well-drained substrate. In planters, use a succulent substrate.
34.care: It is a very low-maintenance, drought-tolerant plant. Standing water should be avoided, especially in winter. The pink tones are most intense in full sun.

faq.q: Where should Sedum 'Watson' be planted?
faq.a: In full sun, in rock gardens, planters and on green roofs, on a well-drained substrate.

faq.q: Why do the rosettes lose their pink colour?
faq.a: In shade the colour becomes greener; the pink tones are only intense in full sun.

35.uses: Hylotelephium spectabile (formerly Sedum spectabile) is a robust perennial with fleshy leaves and flat pink flower heads from late summer to autumn. It is an excellent nectar plant, attracting bees and butterflies, and is used in sunny beds, borders, naturalistic gardens and low-maintenance public spaces.
35.planting: Plant 5–7 plants per square metre in full sun and well-drained soil. It does not need rich soil – in overly fertile soils the stems flop.
35.care: It is very drought tolerant. Dry flower heads can be left over winter as they are decorative, and in spring the stems are cut to ground level. It needs no fertiliser.

faq.q: When does Sedum spectabile flower?
faq.a: From late summer to autumn, usually August–October.

faq.q: Why do Sedum spectabile stems flop?
faq.a: Most often because the soil is too rich or the site too shady; the plant prefers poor soils and full sun.

36.uses: Lamb's ear (Stachys byzantina) is loved for its soft, silvery, woolly leaves, which brighten beds and contrast beautifully with green or purple foliage. It is used as ground cover and edging in sunny sites, gravel gardens, sensory gardens and Mediterranean schemes.
36.planting: Plant 6–9 plants per square metre in full sun and dry, well-drained soil. It spreads, forming a silver carpet over time.
36.care: It tolerates drought very well but dislikes excessive wet in winter. For a more compact leaf carpet, flower stems can be removed. Damaged leaves are cleaned up in spring.

faq.q: Where should lamb's ear be planted?
faq.a: In full sun, in dry, well-drained soil, as edging or ground cover.

faq.q: Is Stachys byzantina drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most drought-tolerant perennials; the main problem is excessive moisture.

37.uses: The olive tree (Olea europaea) instantly brings a Mediterranean feel to restaurant and hotel terraces, courtyards, building entrances and winter gardens. Its silvery-green evergreen foliage and the gnarled trunks of mature specimens make it a sought-after design element in hospitality and premium residential projects.
37.planting: Olive trees only withstand short frosts down to about -10°C. In most of Romania they are grown in large pots or planters with a well-drained substrate; planting directly in the ground is only possible in regions with very mild winters, in sheltered sites.
37.care: In summer it needs full sun and moderate watering, without standing water in the pot. In winter, potted specimens are kept in a bright, cool place (about 5–10°C) or protected with fleece in sheltered spots. The crown can be shaped by pruning at the end of winter.

faq.q: Can an olive tree stay outdoors in winter in Romania?
faq.a: Only in regions with mild winters and with protection; generally, growing it in a pot and overwintering it in a bright, cool place is recommended.

faq.q: Are olive trees suitable for restaurant terraces?
faq.a: Yes, in large pots they are among the most sought-after trees for terraces and Mediterranean-style hospitality venues.

38.uses: A bonsai is a miniature tree shaped through special pruning and training techniques. It is an elegant decorative element for offices, hotel receptions, restaurants, shops and terraces, and a distinctive corporate gift. Depending on the species, there are indoor and outdoor bonsai.
38.planting: Bonsai are grown in special shallow pots with bonsai substrate, which provides good drainage and aeration. Placement depends on the species: indoor species need plenty of light, while outdoor species must be kept outside and protected only from severe frost.
38.care: Watering is the most important factor: the substrate must not dry out completely, and in summer daily watering may be needed. The shape is maintained by pinching shoots and periodic pruning. Every 2–3 years the bonsai is repotted into fresh substrate.

faq.q: Should a bonsai be kept indoors or outdoors?
faq.a: It depends on the species: some are indoor species, others must be kept outdoors all year. We will recommend the right species for your space.

faq.q: How often should a bonsai be watered?
faq.a: When the top layer of the substrate starts to dry; in summer daily watering may be needed.

39.uses: Leyland cypress (× Cuprocyparis leylandii) is the fastest-growing conifer for tall hedges, windbreaks and privacy screens around properties, warehouses, industrial zones and residential developments. In just a few years it can form a tall, dense green wall that shields from wind, dust and view.
39.planting: For hedges, 1.5–2 plants per linear metre are usually planted (50–70 cm apart), depending on plant size. It adapts to various soil types but does not tolerate waterlogging. After planting, tall plants are staked.
39.care: It grows very fast (60–100 cm per year), so the hedge is trimmed two or three times a year, from spring to late summer. Important: do not cut into old wood without needles, as it will not regrow from there. It is hardy to about -15°C.

faq.q: How fast does Leyland cypress grow?
faq.a: It grows about 60–100 cm per year, making it one of the fastest conifers for tall hedges.

faq.q: Can Leyland cypress be cut back hard?
faq.a: No – cuts into old wood without needles do not regrow. The hedge should be trimmed regularly, 2–3 times a year, from the first year.

40.uses: Gaura (Gaura lindheimeri) is an airy perennial with fine stems and small white or pink flowers that seem to float above the plant like butterflies. It flowers for a very long time, from June until autumn, and is used in naturalistic beds, gravel gardens, roundabouts and drought-resistant green spaces.
40.planting: Plant 5–7 plants per square metre in full sun and well-drained soil. It has a deep taproot that helps it withstand drought but makes it hard to move once established.
40.care: It is very drought- and heat-tolerant and needs no fertiliser. Excess winter wet is the main risk, so drainage is essential. Stems are cut back in spring to 10–15 cm above the ground.

faq.q: How long does Gaura flower?
faq.a: It flowers continuously from June until autumn, one of the longest flowering periods among perennials.

faq.q: Is Gaura drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, thanks to its deep taproot it tolerates drought and heat very well.

41.uses: Evergreen candytuft (Iberis sempervirens) is an evergreen perennial subshrub that is completely covered with white flowers in spring. It is used in borders, rock gardens, retaining walls, planters and as ground cover in sunny sites, staying green in winter.
41.planting: Plant 7–9 plants per square metre in full sun and well-drained soil. It also tolerates calcareous soils.
41.care: After flowering, plants are lightly trimmed to stay compact and dense. In dry periods it needs moderate watering. It is hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: When does Iberis flower?
faq.a: Iberis sempervirens flowers in spring, usually in April–May.

faq.q: Does Iberis keep its leaves in winter?
faq.a: Yes, it is evergreen and stays green all year.

42.uses: Common lilac (Syringa vulgaris) is the classic flowering shrub of Central and Eastern European gardens, with large, intensely fragrant flower clusters in April–May. It is used as a solitary shrub, in groups, as an informal flowering hedge and in parks, school yards and traditional gardens. It is extremely frost-hardy and long-lived.
42.planting: As an informal hedge, plant one shrub every 1–1.5 m; as a solitary shrub leave 2–3 m of space. It prefers sunny sites – in shade it flowers poorly – and tolerates calcareous soils.
42.care: Pruning is done right after flowering, as next year's flower buds form in summer. Spent flower clusters are removed, and suckers from the base are cut periodically. Once established it needs very little care.

faq.q: When should lilac be pruned?
faq.a: Right after flowering; pruning in autumn or winter removes the flower buds.

faq.q: Why is my lilac not flowering?
faq.a: The most common causes are deep shade and pruning at the wrong time.

43.uses: Crape myrtle (Lagerstroemia indica) is an exotic shrub with crinkled flowers in pink, red, purple or white from July to September, when few shrubs are still in flower. In autumn the leaves turn orange and red, and its decorative bark peels. It is used as a solitary shrub, trained as a standard, in urban plantings, on terraces and in Mediterranean gardens.
43.planting: Hardy to about -15°C, crape myrtle does best in regions with mild winters, in sunny, warm sites sheltered from cold winds. It prefers well-drained soils. Planting is done in spring.
43.care: It comes into leaf late, only at the end of spring. Flowers appear on new wood, so pruning is done at the end of winter. Young plants are protected in their first winters by mulching the base.

faq.q: Can Lagerstroemia survive Romanian winters?
faq.a: It is hardy to about -15°C, so it suits mainly regions with mild winters and sheltered sites.

faq.q: When does Lagerstroemia flower?
faq.a: It flowers from July to September, on the current year's growth.

44.uses: Italian cypress (Cupressus sempervirens) is the emblematic columnar conifer of Mediterranean landscapes. Its slender silhouettes create strong vertical accents along avenues, at entrances, in courtyards, cemeteries and Italian- or Tuscan-style gardens, as well as in premium residential projects.
44.planting: Plant in rows 1–1.5 m apart for avenues and screens, or individually as a vertical accent. It prefers full sun, warmth and well-drained soils; heavy, wet soils should be avoided. Hardy to about -15°C, it is best suited to regions with mild winters and sheltered sites.
44.care: Once established it tolerates drought very well. In the first years water during dry spells and protect from cold winter winds. Its natural columnar shape needs no pruning.

faq.q: Can Italian cypress survive Romanian winters?
faq.a: It is hardy to about -15°C; it suits regions with mild winters and sites sheltered from cold winds.

faq.q: How far apart should Italian cypress be planted?
faq.a: For avenues and rows, 1–1.5 m between plants.

45.uses: Japanese cherry (Prunus serrulata) is one of the most spectacular flowering ornamental trees: in April the crown is covered with pink or white, often double flowers. It is an attraction in parks, street plantings, squares, school yards and residential developments, and in autumn its leaves turn orange and red.
45.planting: At maturity it reaches 6–8 m in height with a broad crown. In avenues it is planted 6–8 m apart. It prefers full sun and fertile, well-drained soils without standing water.
45.care: After planting, trees are staked and watered regularly for the first two years. Pruning is limited to removing dead or crossing branches and is done after flowering or in summer to reduce the risk of disease.

faq.q: When does Japanese cherry flower?
faq.a: Japanese cherry flowers in April for about two weeks, depending on the variety and the weather.

faq.q: Is Japanese cherry suitable for street plantings?
faq.a: Yes, thanks to its medium size and spectacular flowering it is widely used in avenues and parks.

46.uses: Japanese maple (Acer palmatum) is an elegant ornamental tree with finely cut leaves in purple-red or green that colour spectacularly in autumn. It is the centrepiece of Japanese gardens and modern landscaping, courtyards, entrances and terraces, where it is also grown in large containers.
46.planting: It prefers partial shade and sites sheltered from wind and strong afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves. It needs rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soils.
46.care: In hot summers it needs regular watering; mulching keeps moisture in and protects the shallow roots. It grows slowly and needs no pruning apart from removing dead branches, in late autumn or winter.

faq.q: Why do Japanese maple leaves scorch in summer?
faq.a: Because of strong sun, wind or lack of water; Japanese maple prefers partial shade and consistently moist soil.

faq.q: Can Japanese maple be grown in a container?
faq.a: Yes, it is very well suited to large containers on terraces, with a well-drained substrate and regular watering.

47.uses: The windmill palm (Trachycarpus fortunei) is one of the few frost-hardy palms, suitable for outdoor planting in many regions. Its large fan-shaped leaves and fibre-covered trunk bring an exotic touch to hotel and restaurant terraces, pools, courtyards and Mediterranean gardens.
47.planting: It is hardy to about -12°C, and well-established mature specimens can tolerate short, harder frosts. Plant in sunny or partly shaded sites sheltered from cold winds, in well-drained soil. It is also suitable for large containers.
47.care: In summer it needs moderate watering. In severe winters, young specimens are protected: the leaves are tied upwards and the trunk and crown are wrapped in fleece. Old, dry leaves are cut off at the base.

faq.q: Can a Trachycarpus palm stay outdoors in winter?
faq.a: Yes, in many regions, with protection in severe winters, especially for young specimens.

faq.q: How is a palm protected in winter?
faq.a: The leaves are tied upwards and the trunk and crown are wrapped in fleece during hard frosts.

48.uses: Sago palm (Cycas revoluta) is a very ancient exotic plant with stiff, feathery leaves arranged in a rosette on a thick trunk. It is a striking decorative element for terraces, hotel lobbies, offices, restaurants, pools and winter gardens, usually grown in pots.
48.planting: It only withstands light frosts down to about -8°C, so in Romania it is grown in pots with a very well-drained substrate. In summer it can stay outdoors in sun or partial shade; in winter it is moved to a bright, frost-free space.
48.care: It grows very slowly, usually producing just one new crown of leaves per year. Water moderately, letting the substrate dry between waterings; overwatering leads to rot. Note: all parts of the plant are toxic, so keep it away from children and pets.

faq.q: Can Cycas revoluta stay outdoors in winter?
faq.a: Not in most of Romania; it is hardy only to about -8°C and should be overwintered in a bright, frost-free space.

faq.q: Is Cycas revoluta toxic?
faq.a: Yes, all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, especially the seeds; it should be placed away from children and pets.

49.uses: Japanese cherry 'Royal Burgundy' combines two rare qualities: dark purple foliage from spring to autumn and abundant double pink flowers in April. It is used in residential street plantings, parks, school yards, residential developments and private gardens, as a focal point or to contrast with green foliage.
49.planting: At maturity it reaches about 6–8 m in height with a vase-shaped crown. In avenues it is planted 5–7 m apart. It prefers full sun and fertile, well-drained soils without standing water. Plant in autumn or spring and stake.
49.care: In the first two years after planting it needs regular watering. Pruning is limited to dead or crossing branches and is done after flowering or in summer to reduce the risk of disease. It is hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: When does Japanese cherry 'Royal Burgundy' flower?
faq.a: It flowers in April with double pink blossoms that contrast beautifully with the purple leaves.

faq.q: How big does 'Royal Burgundy' grow?
faq.a: Usually 6–8 m tall with a vase-shaped crown, also suitable for medium-width streets.

50.uses: The silk tree (Albizia julibrissin) brings an exotic touch to gardens, hotel and restaurant terraces, courtyards and parks. Its fine, fern-like foliage gives light shade, and the fluffy pink flowers appear from June to August, when few trees are still in bloom.
50.planting: It forms a broad, umbrella-shaped crown of 6–8 m. It prefers warm, sunny sites sheltered from cold winds and well-drained soils. Plant in spring so it can root before winter.
50.care: Once established it tolerates drought and heat well. Young plants are protected in their first winters by mulching the base. It comes into leaf late, only at the end of spring – this is normal for the species. Prune at the end of winter.

faq.q: Can Albizia survive Romanian winters?
faq.a: Mature trees withstand frosts down to about -15°C; in cold regions sheltered sites and protection of young plants are recommended.

faq.q: When does Albizia flower?
faq.a: From June to August, with fluffy pink powder-puff flowers.

51.uses: The multi-stem form of the silk tree has several trunks rising from the base and a broad, airy crown. It is a striking specimen for terraces, building entrances, courtyards, modern gardens and hospitality venues where a sculptural plant element is wanted.
51.planting: Plant as a specimen with enough room for the broad crown. It prefers full sun, warmth and well-drained soils. Plant in spring in sites sheltered from cold winter winds.
51.care: It tolerates drought once established and needs no formative pruning – only dead or crossing branches are removed. Protect the base of young plants in their first winters.

faq.q: What is the difference between single-stem and multi-stem Albizia?
faq.a: The multi-stem form has several trunks from the base and a wider, lower crown, and is used mainly as a decorative specimen.

faq.q: Where does a multi-stem Albizia fit best?
faq.a: On terraces, at entrances, in courtyards and modern gardens, as a sculptural element.

52.uses: The large-leaved lime (Tilia platyphyllos) is a classic tree for wide avenues, parks, squares and churchyards. Its broad crown gives dense summer shade, and the June flowers fill the air with fragrance and are an important nectar source for bees.
52.planting: At maturity it exceeds 25 m in height, so it needs space: in avenues it is planted 8–12 m apart. It prefers fertile, deep, moist soils and tolerates calcareous soils. Plant in autumn or spring and stake.
52.care: In the first years water regularly and carry out formative pruning to raise the crown. It is very frost-hardy (to about -30°C) and long-lived. In very dry summers it may drop its leaves early.

faq.q: When does the large-leaved lime flower?
faq.a: It is the first lime to flower, usually in June, with fragrant blossoms valuable for bees.

faq.q: How far apart are limes planted in avenues?
faq.a: Usually 8–12 m, as they form a very broad crown at maturity.

53.uses: The small-leaved lime (Tilia cordata) is one of the most widely used street trees in Europe. It tolerates compacted soils, pollution and urban conditions, responds well to pruning and forms a dense, regular crown. It suits avenues, parks, car parks and school yards.
53.planting: It reaches 20–25 m in height. In avenues it is usually planted 8–10 m apart. It adapts to most soils, preferring fertile, moist ones. Plant in autumn or spring with staking and trunk protection.
53.care: Water regularly in the first 2–3 years. Formative pruning raises the crown for pedestrians and vehicles. It is very frost-hardy (to about -30°C). The June–July flowers are excellent for bees.

faq.q: Why is small-leaved lime so common on streets?
faq.a: Because it tolerates urban conditions, responds well to pruning and forms a regular, dense crown.

faq.q: Is small-leaved lime good for bees?
faq.a: Yes, its June–July flowers are a very good nectar source.

54.uses: The silver lime (Tilia tomentosa) stands out with leaves that are white-silver underneath and shimmer in the wind. It tolerates drought, heat and pollution better than other limes, which makes it a very good choice for avenues, parks and public spaces in ever hotter summers.
54.planting: It reaches 20–30 m in height with a broad, regular crown. In avenues it is planted 8–12 m apart. It adapts to various soils, including drier ones. Plant in autumn or spring.
54.care: Once established it tolerates drought well. In the first years water regularly and stake. Formative pruning is done in winter. It flowers later than other limes, usually in July.

faq.q: Is silver lime drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant limes, well suited to cities.

faq.q: When does silver lime flower?
faq.a: Later than other limes, usually in July.

55.uses: Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) is a very hardy conifer, recognisable by the orange bark on the upper trunk. It is used in parks, shelterbelts, afforestation, on slopes and in low-maintenance green spaces, where it thrives on poor, sandy soils.
55.planting: As a specimen it needs space, exceeding 20 m at maturity. For shelterbelts it is planted 3–4 m apart. It prefers sunny sites and well-drained soils and does not tolerate waterlogging.
55.care: Once established it needs very little care and withstands frost and drought. Water only in the first years and during very dry periods. No pruning is needed except for dead branches.

faq.q: Which soils does Scots pine grow on?
faq.a: It tolerates poor and sandy soils very well, provided they are well drained.

faq.q: Is Scots pine suitable for shelterbelts?
faq.a: Yes, it is resistant to wind, frost and drought and is often used in shelterbelts and afforestation.

56.uses: Red oak (Quercus rubra) grows faster than most oaks and has one of the most beautiful autumn colours, in shades of bright red. It is used in large parks, wide avenues, campuses and public green spaces.
56.planting: At maturity it reaches 20–25 m with a broad crown. In avenues it is planted 10–12 m apart. It prefers acidic to neutral soils; on very calcareous soils the leaves can turn yellow. Plant in autumn or spring.
56.care: In the first years water regularly and stake. Formative pruning is done in winter. It is very frost-hardy (to about -30°C) and tolerates urban conditions well.

faq.q: When does red oak change colour?
faq.a: In autumn, usually in October, the leaves turn bright red to reddish-brown.

faq.q: Which soils does red oak need?
faq.a: It prefers acidic to neutral soils; on very calcareous soils the leaves may yellow.

57.uses: Sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua) is valued for its star-shaped leaves and spectacular autumn colour, which runs through yellow, orange, red and purple. It is used in parks, avenues, residential developments and as a specimen tree.
57.planting: It has a regular pyramidal crown and usually reaches 15–20 m in cultivation. In avenues it is planted 8–10 m apart. It prefers moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soils. Plant in spring or autumn.
57.care: In the first years it needs regular watering. The spiky round fruits drop in autumn and winter – worth considering next to pavements and car parks. Pruning is limited to dead branches.

faq.q: Why is sweetgum so popular?
faq.a: For its star-shaped leaves and spectacular red, purple and orange autumn colour.

faq.q: Does sweetgum produce fruit?
faq.a: Yes, spiky round fruits that drop in autumn and winter; worth considering near paths and car parks.

58.uses: The tulip tree (Liriodendron tulipifera) is an imposing tree with unusually shaped leaves, 'cut off' at the tip, yellow-green and orange tulip-like flowers in June and golden-yellow autumn colour. It suits large parks, botanical gardens, campuses and wide avenues.
58.planting: It grows fast and reaches 25–30 m, so it needs a lot of space: as a specimen or in avenues 10–12 m apart. It prefers fertile, deep, moist soils. Plant in spring.
58.care: Water regularly in the first years, especially in dry summers. It is frost-hardy (to about -30°C). Pruning is limited to shaping the crown and removing dead branches.

faq.q: Why is it called the tulip tree?
faq.a: Because of its flowers, which resemble tulips, and its tulip-shaped leaves.

faq.q: How big does the tulip tree grow?
faq.a: It is a large tree reaching 25–30 m, suited to parks and spacious sites.

59.uses: Norway maple 'Crimson King' (Acer platanoides) keeps its deep crimson-purple leaves from spring to autumn, giving strong contrast with green-leaved trees. It is widely used in avenues, parks, residential developments and commercial sites.
59.planting: It reaches 10–15 m in height with a dense, rounded crown. In avenues it is planted 8–10 m apart. It adapts to most soils and tolerates urban conditions. Plant in autumn or spring.
59.care: In the first years water regularly and stake. Formative pruning is done in late summer or winter, avoiding spring, when maples 'bleed' sap. It is very frost-hardy.

faq.q: Does 'Crimson King' keep its colour all summer?
faq.a: Yes, the leaves stay deep crimson-purple from spring to autumn.

faq.q: Is 'Crimson King' suitable for streets?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates urban conditions and forms a dense, rounded crown suited to avenues.

60.uses: Saucer magnolia (Magnolia × soulangeana) is one of the most spectacular spring-flowering plants: in April, before the leaves appear, it is covered with large, cup-shaped white-and-pink flowers. It is an ideal specimen for gardens, building entrances, parks and prestige spaces.
60.planting: It usually reaches 4–8 m in height and width. It prefers sunny or partly shaded sites sheltered from cold winds and rich, slightly acidic to neutral soils. Plant in spring.
60.care: It needs regular watering in the first years and mulching, as its roots are shallow. Late spring frosts can damage the flowers but not the plant. Keep pruning to a minimum, after flowering.

faq.q: When does saucer magnolia flower?
faq.a: In April, before the leaves appear, with large white-and-pink flowers.

faq.q: What happens if magnolia flowers are hit by frost?
faq.a: Late frosts can brown that year's flowers, but the plant itself is not harmed and flowers normally the next year.

61.uses: The purple-leaf cherry plum is one of the most widely used small trees with coloured foliage. Its red-purple leaves contrast with green planting, and in March–April the tree is covered with pink flowers. It is used in narrow streets, parks, school yards, residential developments and as an informal or clipped hedge.
61.planting: It reaches 5–7 m in height with a rounded crown. In avenues it is planted 5–6 m apart, and 50–70 cm apart for hedges. It adapts to most soils, including calcareous ones, and tolerates urban conditions. Leaf colour is most intense in full sun.
61.care: A robust species, frost- and drought-tolerant once established. Water regularly in the first years. Formative pruning is done after flowering; as a hedge it can be trimmed once or twice a year.

faq.q: When does the purple-leaf cherry plum flower?
faq.a: In early spring, usually March–April, with pale pink flowers.

faq.q: Can it be used as a hedge?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates trimming well and can form informal or clipped hedges with red foliage.

62.uses: Box is the traditional plant of formal gardens: path edging, parterres, low hedges and topiary (balls, cones, spirals). It stays green all year and is used at building entrances, in historic gardens, hotel courtyards and decorative pots on terraces.
62.planting: For low edging plant 5–8 plants per linear metre, and 3–4 per metre for taller hedges, depending on size. It tolerates sun and shade and calcareous soils but needs good drainage.
62.care: It grows slowly and is trimmed once or twice a year, usually in early summer. Box can be attacked by the box tree moth and some fungal diseases, so plantings should be checked regularly and treated when needed. Regular watering in dry spells keeps the foliage dense.

faq.q: How many box plants per metre of edging?
faq.a: For low edging, usually 5–8 plants per linear metre, depending on plant size.

faq.q: How do you protect box from the box tree moth?
faq.a: By checking plants regularly in spring and summer and applying specific treatments at the first signs of attack.

63.uses: Red maple is valued for year-round colour: small red flowers before the leaves, green foliage in summer and bright red autumn colour. It is used in avenues, parks, campuses, residential developments and as a specimen tree.
63.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with an oval crown. In avenues it is planted 8–10 m apart. It prefers acidic to neutral, moist soils; on very calcareous soils the leaves can yellow (chlorosis). Plant in autumn or spring.
63.care: Water regularly in the first years, especially in summer. Formative pruning is done in late summer or winter, not in spring. It is very frost-hardy (to about -30°C).

faq.q: When does red maple change colour?
faq.a: In autumn, usually in October, the leaves turn bright red.

faq.q: Which soils does red maple need?
faq.a: It prefers acidic to neutral, moist soils; on very calcareous soils the leaves may yellow.

64.uses: The London plane is one of the toughest trees for cities: it tolerates pollution, compacted soils, heat and pruning, including roof-trained and pollarded forms. It is used on boulevards, squares, parks, school yards and car parks, where it gives dense shade.
64.planting: A large tree reaching 25–35 m with a broad crown. In avenues it is planted 10–15 m apart; for trained (pruned) forms the spacing can be smaller. It adapts to most soils. Plant in autumn or spring and stake.
64.care: Water regularly in the first years. It responds very well to formative and maintenance pruning, done in winter. In wet springs it can lose some leaves to a fungal disease but recovers during the summer.

faq.q: Why is the London plane used on boulevards?
faq.a: Because it tolerates pollution, heat, compacted soils and pruning very well and gives dense shade.

faq.q: How big does the London plane grow?
faq.a: It is a large tree of 25–35 m with a broad crown; in avenues it is planted 10–15 m apart.

65.uses: The mop-head acacia is one of the most widely used trees for small urban spaces: its compact, spherical crown usually stays within 4–6 m in diameter, so it fits narrow streets, pavements, squares, car parks and building courtyards. It has a neat, geometric look and tolerates drought, heat and poor soils exceptionally well.
65.planting: Plant in avenues 4–6 m apart or in regular groups. It adapts to almost any well-drained soil, including poor or sandy ones, and prefers full sun. Plant in autumn or spring with stakes.
65.care: Once established it needs very little care. The crown is thinned and shortened every few years in winter to keep its spherical shape and reduce the risk of wind breakage. Unlike the common black locust it rarely or never flowers.

faq.q: How wide does the mop-head acacia crown grow?
faq.a: Usually 4–6 m in diameter, which makes it suitable for narrow streets and small spaces.

faq.q: Does the mop-head acacia flower?
faq.a: Very rarely; the 'Umbraculifera' form is grown for its spherical crown, not for flowers.

66.uses: Silver birch is valued for its white bark, decorative all year, and its airy crown that lets light through. It is used in parks, in groups of 3–5 trees, in naturalistic gardens, residential developments and recreation areas, where it creates a bright landscape.
66.planting: It reaches 15–25 m with a relatively narrow crown. It looks best planted in groups, 2–4 m apart. It prefers full sun and light, well-drained soils. As its pollen is allergenic, the site near residential buildings should be chosen carefully.
66.care: It has shallow roots, so it needs regular watering and mulching in the first years and in dry summers. It does not tolerate hard pruning; light pruning is done in late summer or autumn, not spring. It is very frost-hardy.

faq.q: Why is silver birch planted in groups?
faq.a: Because the white trunks and airy crowns are most decorative in groups of 3–5 trees.

faq.q: When should silver birch be pruned?
faq.a: Only lightly, in late summer or autumn; in spring birch bleeds a lot of sap when cut.
